items.content_html:
7" Vinyl Record (2026)
45rpm | edition of 50

ULTRA INFRA [field studies] is a numbered limited edition 7” vinyl record featuring two tracks exploring sound beyond human hearing range. Side A (Above) is a composition of ultrasonic bat echolocations. Side B (Below) features low frequency ground vibrations recorded at the root collars of various species of Colorado trees at ecozones ranging from riparian to alpine. These two tracks are only available on vinyl.

Side A: Above (6:14)
Ultrasonic bat echolocations recorded using an AudioMoth full-spectrum acoustic logger at a sample rate of 250kHz (capturing ultrasonic sound up to 125 kHz), in summer 2025.

Side B: Below (4:23)
Ground vibrations recorded at the root collars of various species of Colorado trees at ecozones ranging from riparian (lower elevation, near a water source) to alpine (near tree line ~10,800 ft) in summer 2026.

The infrasonic range (below human hearing, <20 Hz) was isolated and transposed to make low frequency vibrations audible for human listeners. While the exact sources of the sounds remain speculative, environmental factors such as seismic activity, wind through branches and leaves, xylem flow, insects, and nearby foot, car, and air traffic could be responsible for the captured vibrations.

Recorded using a LOM Geofón and transposed between 12-48 semitones (1-4 octaves).

Release Date: November 6, 2026
Field recording, editing, design, and text by Ben Kinsley
Mastered by Michael Southard, Rumourtone Music LLC
Produced by RealMoreReal

Current/ongoing project (2024-present)
Produced by Grand Central Arts Center, Santa Ana, CA

The Lost Champion is a public, place-based project that memorializes the loss of a national champion tree (Brown-Woolly Fig – Ficus drupacea) that was cut down in Santa Ana—by listening to what remains.

A state or national champion tree is the largest known individual of a specific species, determined through a standardized point system based on height, trunk circumference, and average crown spread. These trees are typically identified through public nomination and maintained in official registers—such as American Forests’ National Champion Tree Program and state-level counterparts like the UFEI California Big Trees Registry —to encourage conservation and appreciation of our largest and most extraordinary trees.

Through guided walks, field recording, and collective attention to five sites across Santa Ana that are currently home to state champion trees, The Lost Champion explores the urban forest as a living ecosystem and listening as a form of memory, care, and witness. The project will culminate in an event at the site of the former national champion tree, incorporating field recordings captured prior to its demise.

Programs are currently in development. Stay tuned and join the GCAC mailing list for announcements, as dates and details will be released soon!

www.grandcentralartcenter.com/ben-kinsley-the-lost-champion

Video (2026)
HD | 4:25 | Subtitle: English

While taking a pee break in the forest, a forager discovers the rare and elusive Microglossum viride, the ‘green earth tongue.’ An encounter between two larger-than-life, sporulating ascomycetes and an amateur mycologist leads the viewer on a journey of noticing, appreciating, and identifying tiny, overlooked, and potentially unnamed funga.

Colorado Currents
MCA Denver
July 24 – November 1, 2026

Curated by Miranda Lash, MCA Denver Ellen Bruss Chief Curator & Leilani Lynch, MCA Denver Curator

The exhibition Colorado Currents brings together recent artworks by twenty-eight artists with ties to Colorado, in the spirit of exploring how Colorado is experienced today. This multigenerational group of artists draw from their personal experiences, research, concerns, and hopes for their hometowns, current homes, or homelands. Their work considers how historical legacies shape the present while imagining ideas that may influence Colorado’s future.

Their artworks address a wide range of topics including Colorado’s indigenous communities; histories of mining, labor, cowboys, and violence; the state’s mountain, desert, and prairie landscapes; close investigations of local flora and fauna; coping with drought and wildfires; pop culture references; shifting cities and neighborhoods; stories of inclusion, exclusion and protest; and responses to recent events. While not comprehensive, together these perspectives offer a kaleidoscopic view of how we understand Colorado during its 150th anniversary of statehood.

THE LOST CHAMPION – MEASURING
activation two of a five-part series

Saturday, September 19 @ 10AM
Meet Location: GCAC Lobby *
This is a free program and includes walking. Please wear comfortable shoes and bring water.

If you joined us for Activation #1, you already know the magic of The Lost Champion —and if you missed it, this is your chance to experience it for yourself!

Join us for the next activation of Ben Kinsley’s artist-in-residence project The Lost Champion on Saturday, September 19, 2026 at 10AM. The Lost Champion – Measuring (Activation #2 of 5) will be in collaboration with Orange County resident Michael Cutchins, a citizen scientist who has measured and submitted Orange County trees to official registers for consideration as State or National Champion trees. We will visit trees he nominated that have now become champions and learn the insight and techniques required in the measurement of trees.

Ben will once again be using specialized microphones placed in the ground to “listen” at the trunks and canopy line, allowing our community to hear the subtle tones the trees are producing—an arresting reminder that trees are living beings communicating with the world around them. Plus, we anticipate a few surprise guests joining us along the way.

Ben Kinsley’s artist-in-residence project, The Lost Champion unfolds through a series of five guided walking experiences—Exploring, Measuring, Living With, Listening, and Remembering—that combine guided observation, shared conversation, and opportunities for field recording, listening, and collective attention. Together, these walks invite participants to notice what is present, what is changing, and what has been lost—and to consider what it means to care for the trees that shape our everyday urban forest environments.

Ben Kinsley’s artists-in-residence is supported in part by The Segerstrom Foundation and The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts.

items.title: Book Review in Comedy Studies
items.summary: Book Review: Contemporary Absurdities, Existential Crises, and Visual Art Edited by Katherine Guinness and Charlotte Kent, Bristol, Intellect Books, 2024…
items.content_html:
Book Review:
Contemporary Absurdities, Existential Crises, and Visual Art
Edited by Katherine Guinness and Charlotte Kent, Bristol, Intellect Books, 2024
by Emma Sullivan in "Comedy Studies"

The title, Contemporary Absurdities, Existential Crises, and Visual Art, couched in familiar academic tripartite, suggests a more conventional book than the one we find within its covers. In the collection’s tracking of the absurd, heterogeneity has been encouraged and the usual academic forms which work to unify and effect coherence are frequently discarded, allowing for a fuller sense of encountering very different minds and approaches. The commitment to the overturning of convention is also reflected in the structure of the edition: ordered by the contributors’ first names rather than the customary surname, and with the Janks Archive of insult humour seeded throughout, ready to ambush the reader; ‘YOU HAVE A FACE LIKE A SLAPPED ARSE’ shouts one page (226).

items.content_html:
THE LOST CHAMPION – EXPLORING
activation one of a five-part series

Ben Kinsley with arborists Rhonda Wood and Humberto Mojica
Saturday, June 27 | 10:00 AM–12:00 PM
Meeting Location: Grand Central Art Center (GCAC), Lobby

This is a free program and includes walking. Please wear comfortable shoes and bring water.

The Lost Champion is a public, place-based project by artist Ben Kinsley that memorializes the loss of a national champion tree (Brown-Woolly Fig – Ficus drupacea) that was cut down in Santa Ana, by listening to what remains.

A state or national champion tree is the largest known individual of a specific species, determined through a standardized point system based on height, trunk circumference, and average crown spread. These trees are typically identified through public nomination and maintained in official registers—such as American Forests’ National Champion Tree Program and state-level counterparts like the UFEI California Big Trees Registry  to encourage conservation and appreciation of our largest and most extraordinary trees.

At the heart of The Lost Champion is a series of five guided walking experiences through Santa Ana’s “urban forest,” each offering a different lens for engaging with trees as living beings, civic landmarks, and carriers of ecological and cultural memory. The walks are themed Exploring, Measuring, Living With, Listening, and Remembering, and include guided observation, shared conversation, and opportunities for field recording and collective attention. Together, these experiences invite participants to consider how we encounter, document, and care for the trees that shape our everyday environments—and what it means to notice what is present, what is changing, and what has been lost.

Through guided walks, field recording, and collective attention to sites across Santa Ana that are currently home to state and national champion trees, The Lost Champion explores the urban forest as a living ecosystem and listening as a form of memory, care, and witness. The project will culminate with activation #5 at the site of the former national champion tree, incorporating field recordings Ben captured prior to its removal.

The remaining four activations in the series are currently in development—stay tuned by singing up for the GCAC email announcements. Dates and details will be released soon.

The Lost Champion is a project led by artist Ben Kinsley, with residency support provided by The Segerstrom Foundation and The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts.

 

ABOUT ACTIVATION #1 GUIDES

Rhonda Wood is President, co-owner, and consulting arborist at Woodworks Tree Preservation, Inc., and an ISA Certified Arborist, ISA Certified Tree Climber, and ISA Tree Risk Assessment Qualified professional (WE-5071AT), with Prescription Pruning credentials. She began her career as a gardener at Disneyland in 1997, became a Topiary Engineer, and in 1999 advanced to certified arborist and climber, helping care for more than 16,000 trees. Over a distinguished tenure at the Disneyland Resort, she served as Tree Assessor, Arborist Manager, and Horticulture Planner, and spent her final decade there as the resort’s first Urban Forester. Rhonda also teaches UCLA Extension’s “Study of Trees” course and is deeply engaged in the profession through leadership and service, including roles with the Western Chapter ISA, the ANSI A300 Committee, tree worker evaluation, post-fire inspection volunteering, and judging regional and national tree climbing championships.

Humberto Mojica is Vice President, co-owner, and consulting arborist at Woodworks Tree Preservation, Inc., and an ISA Certified Arborist, ISA Certified Tree Climber, and ISA Tree Risk Assessment Qualified professional (WE-9670AT), with Prescription Pruning credentials. He spent a decade with Armstrong Growers before joining Disneyland as a gardener in 1997, where he led landscape crews and became a Horticulture Manager in 2003. After studying arboriculture, Humberto became a Certified Arborist and Tree Worker and went on to serve as Arborist Manager for 10 years, helping care for more than 16,000 trees before retiring from the Disneyland Resort in 2023. He also practices woodworking as an artist, preserving wood to carry forward the legacy of trees, and contributes to the field through service including the WCISA Spanish Committee (Arboleros), post-fire tree inspection volunteering, tree worker evaluation, and judging regional and national tree climbing championships.
